common_name: Japanese Lantern Hibiscus (Coral Hibiscus, Fringed Rosemallow)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings once nights stay above 55F; grow in containers and overwinter indoors outside zone 10.

directions: This East African species sends out long arching canes studded with pendant, deeply reflexed red flowers whose petal lobes curl back like a lantern shade. Grow it where the dangling blooms can be viewed from below, such as a hanging basket edge or raised bed. It roots readily from softwood cuttings and flowers nearly year-round in warm humid climates with regular feeding. Prune lightly after flushes to keep the lax stems from becoming leggy.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after frost danger passes; needs frost-free, humid conditions or greenhouse protection.

directions: A rare native Hawaiian tree hibiscus bearing large, lightly fragrant white flowers with prominent red styles, a trait few hibiscus species share. It prefers the broken light of a forest edge rather than full tropical sun and resents salty or very dry sites. Container specimens can be moved indoors near a bright window during cool spells in marginal climates. This species has contributed fragrance genes to many modern tropical hibiscus hybrids.

planting.note: Set out after all frost risk passes; thrives in warm, humid, sheltered sites.

directions: Endemic to a single Kauai valley, this hibiscus produces strongly fragrant white flowers with long pink-tipped staminal columns that open in the evening. It grows best with filtered light and consistent moisture, mimicking the understory of its native wet forest. Give it room to develop into a small multi-trunked tree and avoid windy, exposed locations. Because wild populations are endangered, cultivated plants play a real role in conserving the species.
sources: Hawaii Division of Forestry and Wildlife

planting.note: Start indoors with nicked or soaked seed; transplant out after soil is reliably warm.

directions: Native to tropical Asia, this fast-growing rosemallow produces mauve-pink blooms with a deep maroon center and deeply lobed, almost fringed leaves distinct from common garden hibiscus foliage. Grown as a warm-season annual outside the tropics, it flowers heavily from midsummer until frost. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching and more flowering stems. Seed pods are prickly, so handle spent flowers with gloves when deadheading.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
National Tropical Botanical Garden seed records
Rare seed trade catalogs (e.g., Trade Winds Fruit)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized specimens in fall so roots establish before spring growth begins.

directions: This wild tree peony from southeastern Tibet produces clear golden-yellow, bowl-shaped flowers earlier in spring than most tree peony cultivars, backed by finely divided, almost fern-like foliage. It forms a large woody shrub over time and resents being moved once established, so choose its permanent site carefully. Give it deep, well-drained soil and some afternoon shade in hot climates to extend bloom life. Many breeders use it as a parent for yellow-flowered tree peony hybrids.

planting.note: Divide and plant dormant roots in early fall, eyes just below the soil surface.

directions: Found wild across Mediterranean woodlands from Spain to Turkey, this species peony opens large deep rose-pink cups very early in the peony season, often weeks before garden hybrids. It prefers light open shade reminiscent of its native forest-edge habitat rather than the full baking sun tolerated by Paeonia lactiflora. Leave clumps undisturbed for years, since mature roots flower far more reliably than recent divisions. Foliage senesces by midsummer, so pair it with later-emerging perennials to fill the gap.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall with eyes just under the soil surface; avoid spring transplanting.

directions: Native to the Balkans and Turkey, this species is prized among species-peony collectors for flowers of an unusually saturated scarlet-red rarely seen outside hybrids. The cup-shaped blooms sit above glossy, somewhat leathery leaflets on compact, well-behaved plants. It tolerates more sun and heat than many species peonies and establishes readily in average garden soil. Once settled it needs little care beyond an annual mulch and division every several years only if flowering declines.

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions in early fall; give rich, humus-amended soil similar to its Caucasus forest habitat.

directions: Collected from forest clearings in the Transcaucasus, this species peony is closely related to Paeonia mlokosewitschii but opens slightly earlier with pale yellow to cream flowers set off by vivid red filaments. It appreciates the same woodland-edge conditions as its better-known cousin: dappled light, rich soil, and protection from harsh afternoon sun. Plants are slow to reach flowering size from seed, so division or purchased roots are the practical route for most gardeners. Established clumps are long-lived and need minimal maintenance.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter dormancy.

directions: Ranging wild from central Europe into the Caucasus, this compact bearded species iris is unusual for dying back completely leafless in winter, giving it its name. Violet-purple flowers appear on short, sturdy stems in mid-spring above fans that stay tidy and low through summer. It suits rock gardens and iris borders where taller bearded hybrids would overwhelm the scale. Good drainage is essential, since the rhizomes rot quickly in heavy, wet winter soil.
sources: Species Iris Group of North America (SIGNA)

planting.note: Plant divisions in late summer or early fall; spuria irises resent spring disturbance and sulk for a season after moving.

directions: Native to Turkey and the eastern Mediterranean, this tall spuria-group species produces crisp white flowers brightened by a bold yellow signal patch on each fall. Sword-like foliage stays upright and attractive well after bloom, giving strong vertical structure to a perennial border. Unlike bearded iris, it tolerates somewhat heavier soil and benefits from a deep, infrequent watering routine rather than light frequent irrigation. Established clumps resent disturbance and can be left in place for many years between divisions.
sources: Species Iris Group of North America (SIGNA)
